How Blackjack, Baccarat, and Casino War Handle Ties Differently

Published October 22, 2026 · 8 min read · By the OddsLighthouse Editorial Team

"It's a tie" sounds like the one outcome in a casino game simple enough not to need explaining. In practice, a tied hand triggers a completely different procedure depending on which table you're sitting at, and that procedure is doing real mathematical work in the background. Blackjack, baccarat, and casino war all let a hand land in a dead heat, and each game routes that moment through a different rule — one that gives your money straight back, one that splits your bet into a separate wager with its own long odds, and one that hands you an actual decision with real consequences either way. Knowing which is which changes how you should think about the money sitting on the table when it happens.

Blackjack: a push is a non-event

In blackjack, a tie between your hand and the dealer's is called a push, and it's about as uneventful as a casino outcome can be: your original bet is returned to you in full, no win, no loss, no fee taken out along the way. If you wagered $25 and both you and the dealer land on 19, that $25 goes right back into your stack and the next hand deals as if nothing happened. A push doesn't move the house edge in either direction for that hand — it simply removes that round from the win/loss column entirely, which is part of why blackjack's overall house edge is as low as it is under good rules and correct strategy.

There's one well-known wrinkle: a player blackjack (an ace plus a ten-value card) beats a dealer total of 21 made with three or more cards at most tables, so not every "both hands equal 21" situation is actually a push — the two-card blackjack wins outright unless the dealer also has a natural blackjack, in which case it's a true push. For the full mechanics of how a natural interacts with dealer action, see our blackjack basic strategy guide.

Baccarat: the main bet pushes, but the tie bet is its own game

Baccarat looks similar to blackjack on the surface — if the banker's hand and the player's hand finish with the same point total, anyone who bet on Banker or Player gets their wager back, exactly like a blackjack push. That's where the resemblance ends. Most baccarat tables also offer a side wager called the Tie bet, which pays out specifically when the hand ends in a tie, typically at 8 to 1. That sounds generous next to a 1-to-1 payout on Banker or Player, but ties are genuinely rare — they happen on roughly 1 in 11 hands with an eight-deck shoe — and the math behind that payout leaves the house with a steep edge of around 14.4%, among the worst bets at a baccarat table.

The distinction matters because the Tie bet isn't a side effect of the hand pushing — it's a completely separate wager you choose to place before the cards come out, with its own standalone house edge that has nothing to do with how good or bad the Banker and Player bets are. For a deeper look at how that number compares with baccarat's other side wagers, see our guide to baccarat side bets.

OutcomeWhat happens to your Banker/Player betWhat happens to a separate Tie bet, if placed
Banker or Player winsPays out normally (Banker pays 19:20 after commission; Player pays 1:1)Loses
TiePushes — stake returned in fullPays roughly 8:1, house edge near 14.4%

Casino war: a tie hands you a real decision

Casino war strips the card game down to its simplest form — you and the dealer each get one card, and the higher card wins. When the two cards match in rank, you're not handed your money back automatically the way you would be in blackjack or baccarat. Instead, the game gives you an actual choice: surrender and take back half your original bet, or "go to war" by placing an additional bet equal to your original wager, after which a new card is burned and you and the dealer each draw one more card to settle the tie.

That decision isn't cosmetic. If you always surrender on a tie, the house edge on casino war runs close to 3.5%. If you always go to war instead, the edge drops to roughly 2.9%, because going to war comes with a tie-breaker bonus built into most casino war rule sets: if you tie again on the war card and the game ultimately resolves in your favor through that bonus structure, you're paid slightly better than even money on the additional bet. Surrendering is the more conservative, lower-variance path; going to war is the better long-run choice purely on expected value, assuming you can tolerate the extra money and the extra card draw it takes to get there. We cover the full rule set and bonus payout structure in our casino war basics guide.

The key difference: blackjack and baccarat's main bets treat a tie as "nothing happened, here's your money back," while casino war treats a tie as a fresh decision point with its own separate house edge attached to whichever option you pick.

A worked example across all three games

Say you bet $20 at each of the three games in a single session, and each one happens to land on a tie. At blackjack, you simply get your $20 back and move to the next hand — no further action needed. At baccarat, if that $20 was on Banker or Player, it also comes straight back; but if you'd additionally placed a separate $5 wager on the Tie bet, that $5 now pays roughly $40 (8 to 1), a genuinely good outcome for a bet you'll see win far less often than you'll see it lose. At casino war, your $20 tie forces an active choice: take $10 back and walk away from the hand, or put up another $20 and draw again, with a decent chance of a tie-breaker bonus if things go your way on the second card.

Three tied hands, three completely different things happening to your money, even though "it's a tie" describes all three in plain English.

Why this matters for variance, not just edge

House edge gets most of the attention in casino math, but how a game resolves a tie also shapes how choppy your session feels. Blackjack's push mechanic smooths out variance by simply removing dead-heat hands from the equation — your bankroll doesn't move at all on those hands, for better or worse. Baccarat's Tie bet does the opposite on purpose: it's a high-variance side wager that occasionally delivers an 8-to-1 swing specifically because its payout structure is built around a rare event. Casino war sits in between, handing you a real choice between locking in a smaller, certain loss or accepting a bigger, variable outcome on the next card. None of that changes which game has the best headline house edge, but it does change how a session's bankroll swings feel while you're playing. Our casino bankroll management guide covers how to size bets around exactly this kind of variance difference.

Common misconceptions

A common mistake is assuming that because baccarat's main bet pushes on a tie just like blackjack's does, the Tie bet itself must carry a similarly reasonable house edge — it doesn't, and the two are unrelated wagers sitting on the same table. Another is assuming "going to war" in casino war is the riskier, worse play simply because it means putting more money on the table; on a pure expected-value basis, it's actually the better long-run choice of the two options, even though surrendering feels safer in the moment. A third misconception is treating any "both hands equal" situation in blackjack as an automatic push without checking whether one side has a two-card natural blackjack, which changes the outcome entirely rather than resulting in a tie.

Frequently asked questions

Does a blackjack push count as a loss for the purposes of a casino bonus's wagering requirement?

It depends on the operator's specific terms, but a push typically doesn't count as a loss, since no money actually changed hands. Some wagering requirements only count the bet amount toward the rollover regardless of outcome, so check the specific bonus terms rather than assuming.

Is the baccarat Tie bet ever worth playing?

Mathematically, it's one of the worse regular wagers available at a baccarat table, with a house edge around 14.4% compared to roughly 1.06% on Banker and 1.24% on Player. Some players use it occasionally for the bigger payout swing, but it isn't a bet that holds up well over a long session.

In casino war, is surrendering ever the smarter choice despite the worse long-run edge?

It can make sense for a player prioritizing lower variance or managing a tighter bankroll over a session, since surrendering locks in a known, smaller loss instead of risking more money on the next card. It's a reasonable trade-off for comfort, just not the mathematically optimal one.

Why don't more table games just return your bet on every tie, the way blackjack does?

Returning the stake on a tie, as blackjack does, removes an opportunity for the house to build in extra edge around that outcome. Games like baccarat and casino war instead turn the tie into its own wagering decision or side bet, which is simply a more profitable design for the house than a flat push would be.
